content: 1. Antiretroviral drugs have either failed to achieve their intended therapeutic outcomes or have caused unacceptable levels of toxicity or adverse side effects in some cases. 2. A study conducted in France examined a cohort of 1,754 uninfected infants born to HIV-1-infected women who received antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy. Among these infants, eight developed signs of mitochondrial dysfunction within the first few months of life. Four of these infants had in utero or neonatal exposure to ZDV-3TC, and the other four were exposed to ZDV alone. 3. Of the eight infants with mitochondrial dysfunction, two (both exposed to ZDV-3TC) developed severe neurologic disease and subsequently died. Three infants exhibited mild to moderate symptoms, while the remaining three were asymptomatic but showed transient laboratory abnormalities. 4. A definitive causal relationship between in utero exposure to antiretroviral drugs and mitochondrial dysfunction has not been established. 5. In the PACTG 076 study, which followed infants up to 18 months of age, neurologic events were rare. Seizures occurred in one child exposed to ZDV and two children exposed to placebo. Spasticity was reported in one child from each group. 6. In a database of over 16,000 uninfected children born to HIV-1-infected women, no deaths or clinical findings attributable to mitochondrial dysfunction were identified. Most infants with antiretroviral exposure had been exposed to ZDV alone, with only about 6% exposed to ZDV-3TC. 7. In the African PETRA trial, which compared three ZDV-3TC regimens to placebo for preventing HIV transmission, no increased risk of neurologic adverse events was observed among the 1,798 children studied, regardless of the intensity of treatment. 8. A study of 382 uninfected infants born to HIV-1-infected women included echocardiograms performed every 4 to 6 months during the first five years of life. Nine percent of these infants had prenatal exposure to ZDV. No significant differences in ventricular function were observed between infants exposed to ZDV and those who were not. 9. Even if a link between mitochondrial dysfunction and in utero antiretroviral exposure is confirmed, the occurrence of severe or fatal mitochondrial disease in these infants appears to be extremely rare. This risk must be weighed against the clear benefit of ZDV in reducing HIV transmission by nearly 70%. 10. These findings underscore the importance of the existing Public Health Service recommendation for long-term follow-up of children with in utero exposure to antiretroviral drugs. 11. Healthcare providers treating HIV-1-infected pregnant women and their newborns are strongly encouraged to report cases of prenatal antiretroviral drug exposure to the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry. This registry collects observational, non-experimental data to assess the potential teratogenicity of these drugs. 12. Data from the registry supplement animal toxicology studies and assist clinicians in evaluating the risks and benefits of antiretroviral treatment for individual patients. The registry is a collaborative effort involving pharmaceutical manufacturers and an advisory committee of obstetric and pediatric practitioners. 13. The registry does not use patient names, and follow-up information on birth outcomes is obtained from the reporting physician. 14. Final results from the PACTG 076 study, which included 419 infants, demonstrated a 66% reduction in the risk of HIV transmission among those who received ZDV compared to placebo. 15. The mechanism by which ZDV reduces HIV transmission in PACTG 076 participants has not been fully elucidated. The effect of ZDV on maternal HIV-1 RNA levels does not entirely explain its observed efficacy. 16. Pre-exposure prophylaxis of the fetus or infant may provide substantial protection, and transplacental passage of antiretroviral drugs is likely crucial for preventing transmission. 17. Placental perfusion studies have shown that ZDV is metabolized into its active triphosphate form within the placenta, potentially offering additional protection against in utero transmission. 18. In PACTG 076, similar rates of congenital abnormalities were observed among infants with and without in utero ZDV exposure. Data from the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry also indicate no increased risk of congenital abnormalities among infants born to women who received ZDV antenatally compared to the general population. 19. Long-term follow-up of infants exposed to ZDV in utero, including up to six years of age, has shown no differences in growth, neurodevelopment, or immunologic status compared to those born to mothers who received placebo. 20. However, the follow-up period is insufficient to definitively assess the carcinogenic risk associated with human exposure to ZDV. Long-term monitoring remains recommended for all infants with in utero exposure to ZDV or other antiretroviral drugs. 21. The efficacy of ZDV chemoprophylaxis in reducing HIV-1 transmission has also been evaluated in other perinatal protocols, such as PACTG 185, and in prospective cohort studies. PACTG 185 enrolled pregnant women with advanced HIV-1 disease and low CD4+ counts, 24% of whom had received ZDV prior to their current pregnancy.
